title: Eighty years in robes
hook: the elder Bakkula, eighty years a monk and never ill

segments.voice: Yesterday: the birth marvels, and your line, the real marvel. Did you catch the moment a feeling began? Today, a very old monk, and a visit from an old friend. Day four hundred ninety-three.

An old friend turns up after a lifetime apart, and the first thing out of his mouth is a question nobody else would dare ask. That's how the hundred and twenty-fourth discourse begins. The elder Bakkula is staying near Rajagaha. A naked ascetic named Kassapa, a friend from Bakkula's lay days, comes to see him. How long have you been a monk, friend Bakkula? Eighty years. And then Kassapa asks a blunt personal question about desire. Bakkula doesn't answer it the way it's asked. Today: eighty years in robes.
screen: `AN OLD FRIEND, A LIFETIME LATER.` → `HOW LONG A MONK? EIGHTY YEARS.` → `A BLUNT QUESTION.`

segments.voice: You shouldn't ask it that way, Bakkula says. Ask instead: in eighty years, how many times has a thought of sensual desire even come up? And he answers that one: not once. Then, in the discourse, a long list follows, almost like an inventory of a life. In eighty years, he says, he never accepted a robe from a householder; he wore cast-off cloth. He never sat down to an invitation meal. He never leaned against a wall to rest, never lay down on a bed. And then this: in eighty years, he never had an illness, not even for as long as it takes to pull a cow's teat. He never took so much as a piece of medicinal fruit. On the eighth day after he went forth, he says, he was freed. Each item ends with the same refrain from the reciters: and this too we remember as a wonderful quality of the venerable Bakkula. Kassapa is so moved he asks to go forth under him, and in time reaches the goal himself. Then the ending. One day Bakkula takes a key and goes from dwelling to dwelling, saying: come out, venerables. Today I'll pass away. And he does, sitting among the monks. The Buddha never appears in this discourse. Bakkula's way was unusually strict, and plenty of Buddhists, then and now, take medicine, sit at invitations and wear donated robes. What rings true across eighty years is something simpler: a body used carefully, a life kept plain, and a death met sitting up, among friends.
screen: `ASK IT ANOTHER WAY` · `A PLAIN, EIGHTY-YEAR INVENTORY` · `NEVER ILL, NOT EVEN A MOMENT` · `A KEY, AND A QUIET DEATH` · then, large: `EIGHTY YEARS IN ROBES.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: thank your body today. Bodies are different, and not everyone has Bakkula's health, so this isn't about comparing. Sit and settle. Move your attention slowly through the body. Wherever something is working, a hand that holds, lungs that fill, eyes that read, give it a silent thank you. Where something hurts, just acknowledge it carried you here too. The bell holds the time.
Eighty years in robes. The elder Bakkula, eighty years a monk, never ill even for a moment, who met his death sitting among the monks. Today's word.
Your line: eighty years in robes. Today, do one plain, kind thing for your body: water, a walk, an early night, and notice it as care. Day four hundred ninety-three.

howItsDone: In Theravada tradition Bakkula is remembered as the monk foremost in good health, and the rag-robe and solitary practices he kept are among the optional ascetic practices (dhutanga) some forest monks still take up today.

trapdoor: what you thought: a story about a monk who was never sick.
what it means: a plain life, carefully kept, from a reunion question to a death met sitting among friends.
what a scholar hears: MN 124 is narrated without the Buddha, with a refrain of the reciters' praise, and some scholars read it as a later addition to the Middle-Length Sayings.

notes: MN 124 paraphrased and the list shortened. Confirm items: robes from householders, invitation meals, leaning against a support, lying down, illness 'as long as it takes to pull a cow's teat', medicine 'not even a piece of myrobalan', final knowledge on the eighth day.
Kassapa's question concerns sexual intercourse; the script calls it 'a blunt personal question about desire'. Confirm this is an acceptable rendering.
